title: Before you touch a portal, get the principle right
paras: Before you touch a portal, get the principle right. Uploading is the easy part — applications fail because they were put together wrong, or the wrong thing was applied for. So be sure of three things first. And a note up front: the citations and cross-references are in the written guide, not here.

One, you're applying for the right thing. Householder, full, outline, reserved matters, a lawful development certificate, listed building consent, advertisement consent, prior approval, a section 73 variation — each has its own form, fee and requirements, and getting the type wrong loses you weeks. If unsure, use the portal guidance and pre-application service. Two, know your constraints before you design the submission — they drive what you submit and whether the scheme's deliverable. Conservation area, a listed building on or near the site, flood zone, Green Belt, a National Landscape, a tree preservation order, protected species — any one can be a showstopper; and a nutrient-sensitive catchment may need secured mitigation in place first, so read the nutrient neutrality guide.

Three, allow time for the evidence — the biggest cause of delay is documents commissioned too late. Surveys have seasonal windows; you can't do a bat emergence survey in December. Net gain assessments, heritage, drainage, arboriculture and transport all have lead-in. Scope the list at the start, not the week you submit.

title: Where to upload: the portals compared
paras: Now, where to upload. In England there's more than one route, and they're not equivalent — same destination, the local planning authority, but different help along the way. The safe default is the Planning Portal; every English authority accepts it. Only use an alternative once you've confirmed yours takes it too.

Two points. Each commercial portal charges a service fee on top of the statutory planning fee that goes to the council — the Planning Portal's around seventy-five pounds plus VAT, Planda's a little under, though these move, so check on the day. And whichever route you use, validation happens at the authority's end — a portal that pre-checks, like Planda, cuts the chance of a bounce, but it's the council that decides you're valid.

title: What to have ready up front
paras: Have everything ready before you start — half-finishing a form then hunting for a document is how mistakes creep in. Start with the site and who owns it: the precise address, its unique property reference number, and a clear ownership picture. If the applicant doesn't own the whole site, you need the right ownership certificate — A where they own it all, then B, C or D where others have an interest — and you may have to serve notice on other owners and any agricultural tenants. A wrong or unsigned certificate is a standard rejection, and serving notice takes time, so sort it first.

Then the plans — an up-to-date, Ordnance Survey-based location plan and a site plan, to recognised scales. Buy the location plan from an Ordnance Survey-licensed provider; a free-mapping screenshot gets rejected. You'll also need the existing and proposed drawings the proposal requires, each to scale and each with its own number. And the supporting evidence the local list demands: commonly a design and access statement for major and some heritage cases, a heritage statement, a preliminary ecological appraisal and net gain assessment, a flood risk assessment and drainage strategy, an arboricultural report, a transport statement or travel plan, and noise or contamination work. Commission the slow items early.

Then the money. Work out the exact fee on the portal's calculator, and check any exemption or reduction — the reduced fee for certain resubmissions, the exemptions for disabled adaptations. Note whether the Community Infrastructure Levy applies, because you'll usually submit the levy's additional information form with the application, and reliefs must be claimed and confirmed before you start on site. Get the fee exactly right — underpay by a pound and you're invalid. And set up a portal account in advance.

title: The documents: what a valid application contains
paras: What a valid application actually contains. Validity has two layers — the national requirements every application meets, and the local list each authority publishes per type. Miss either and you're invalid.

The national requirements: the completed form for the correct type; a location plan, normally one to twelve fifty or one to twenty-five hundred on a current Ordnance Survey base, site edged red, adjoining land the applicant owns edged blue, a north point and enough named roads to find it; a site or block plan, normally one to five hundred or one to two hundred, showing the development in its plot — buildings, access, parking, boundaries; and the drawings describing the proposal — existing and proposed elevations, floor plans, roof plans and sections at one to fifty or one to a hundred, each to an identified scale, north on plans, its own number and revision. Then the ownership certificate — A, B, C or D — and the agricultural holdings certificate, signed. A design and access statement where required — major development, and development affecting designated heritage assets in the specified circumstances, with listed building consent having its own requirement. Biodiversity net gain information where the mandatory regime applies — the metric and habitat plans — a fire statement for the taller residential buildings that need one, and the correct fee paid in full.

On top sits the local list. The authority can't demand just anything — a requirement is only lawful where it's reasonable to think the information's material to that application type, and reasonable in scale. But within those limits it's real, and an application that ignores it is held invalid. Read the target authority's current local list before you assemble anything; it's the most common thing people get wrong.

title: Step by step: uploading on the Planning Portal
paras: Uploading, step by step. This is the Planning Portal, but Planda and council-direct services follow the same shape, Planda adding checks as you go. Log in and start a new application. Find the site by postcode, address or on the map. Choose the application type — that drives the form and fee, so get it right.

Then work through the form — applicant and agent details, a precise description, materials, trees, foul and surface-water drainage, access and parking, hours and employment where relevant, and the ownership certificate. Write the description carefully; it defines what you're applying for and ends up on the decision notice. Attach the documents — location plan, site plan, the other drawings, the design and access statement and reports, the net gain information, the levy form where it applies — naming files so the drawing numbers match the form.

Calculate and pay the fee through the calculator; the portal pays the authority. Sign the ownership and agricultural holdings certificates and the declaration, and if notice must be served on other owners or tenants, do it and record the dates. Then submit — you get a reference beginning P-P and everything goes over. Keep a full copy of exactly what you submitted, every plan and revision.

title: How to make sure it proceeds (and is not rejected)
paras: How do you make sure it proceeds and isn't rejected? An invalid application isn't registered, and the clock doesn't start until it is — councils return them, and in a busy authority that's weeks gone. Nearly every rejection is off the same short list.

The fee wrong or short — underpayment's the classic, so use the calculator and check any reduction or exemption genuinely applies. The wrong application type. The location plan not to standard — no red line, no blue line where the applicant owns adjoining land, no north point, wrong scale, or not on a current Ordnance Survey base. Drawings not scaled or numbered, or references that don't match the form. Certificates missing, unsigned, or the wrong one for the ownership position. Local-list documents missing — heritage statement, ecology and net gain, flood risk assessment, arboricultural report, transport statement — the single biggest cause of delay. The levy form missing where the levy applies. And a vague or inconsistent description that doesn't match the drawings.

Two habits do most of the work: match the authority's validation checklist item by item before you submit, and when a query comes back, respond fast — they give a limited window to fix things and will dispose of the application if you don't. A portal that pre-validates, like Planda, helps, but the responsibility's yours.

title: After you press submit
paras: After you press submit — submission isn't registration. The authority validates against the national and local requirements first; only then does it register, give a reference, and start the statutory clock. Then the handling process takes over — publicity and consultation, the officer's assessment, and determination within the statutory period, eight weeks for most applications, thirteen for major development, subject to any agreed extension. That's its own guide.

While it runs, stay engaged. Answer any validation query straight away. Watch the consultation responses on the authority's website, and offer amendments if a soluble objection comes up — though a material change can trigger re-consultation. Keep the client informed, and don't assume silence means progress — a polite check-in with the case officer, at sensible intervals, is part of the job.

title: Pre-flight checklist
paras: The pre-flight checklist — run it right before you upload, and if any box is empty, stop. Right application type, matching the proposal? All the constraints checked and dealt with? Ownership settled, the correct certificate signed, notice served on other owners and agricultural tenants with dates recorded?

Location plan on a current Ordnance Survey base, at the right scale, with red line, blue line where relevant, north point and named roads? Site plan at the right scale, in its plot? The other drawings to scale, north on plans, each numbered and revised, matching the form? Local-list documents assembled per the current published list? Net gain information, fire statement and design and access statement each where required? Fee calculated exactly, reductions or exemptions verified, the levy form ready? And a full copy of the submission saved?

title: About the How To series
paras: A word on the series. This is guide one, alongside PlanRef's reference guides, covering the practical tasks. Companions are planned: discharging conditions and the deemed-discharge route; a section 73 or 96A amendment; a lawful development certificate and its evidence; a prior approval, whether Class Q, Class MA or the larger householder route; a section 78 appeal; responding to an enforcement notice; using pre-application advice; and managing the levy. Tell us which you want next.

This covers England, current to July 2026. Portal names, service charges and validation lists all change — so check your target authority's current local validation list, and confirm which route it accepts, before you upload.
